cards.front: Operational risk, Extremfall (99,9%): what fraction of the 3-year average Betriebserträge is the own-funds charge (the CRR Basisindikatoransatz \(\alpha\)-factor)? Give the fraction.

Operational risk, Problemfall (95%): give the derived factor (as a fraction) obtained by rescaling 15% from 99,9% to 95% under the ⅓-normal / ⅔-lognormal mixture, i.e. \(15\%\cdot(0{,}33\cdot\tfrac{1{,}645}{3{,}090}+0{,}67\cdot\tfrac{5{,}180}{21{,}982})\).
EXKURS: with \(\mu=0,\ \sigma=1\) the lognormal 99,9% quantile factor is \(e^{u(0{,}999)}\) where \(u(0{,}999)=3{,}090\). Compute \(e^{3{,}090}\).
The lognormal component's 95%/99,9% VaR ratio: compute \(\tfrac{5{,}180}{21{,}982}\) (the factor that drags the blended op-risk rescaling below the normal-only value).
Probability-weighted 95%/99,9% rescaling ratio for the op-risk mixture: \(0{,}33\cdot\tfrac{1{,}645}{3{,}090}+0{,}67\cdot\tfrac{5{,}180}{21{,}982}\). Give the value (it should land near ⅓).
Worked example: 3-year average Betriebserträge = €20m (from FINREP/VERA). Using the derived Problemfall factor of 5,0%, what is the Problemfall (95%) op-risk charge, in euros?

TRAP: if op-risk loss were treated as purely normal (like CVA), the Problemfall factor would be \(15\%\cdot\tfrac{1{,}645}{3{,}090}\). Give this (incorrect) normal-only factor as a fraction — the value the lognormal tail corrects away from.

To rescale the op-risk charge from 99,9% to 95%, the Leitfaden assumes the loss is a probability-weighted mixture: {{c1}} normally distributed (everyday operational noise) and {{c2}} lognormally distributed (the fat right tail of rare, large losses). This ⅓/⅔ split is an {{c3}} modelling assumption, not a CRR requirement.

EXKURS: if \(Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) then \(X=\exp(Y)\) is lognormal, and because \(\exp(\cdot)\) is strictly increasing its \(p\)-quantile is \(Q_X(p)=\) {{c1}}. With \(\mu=0,\sigma=1\) the multiplicative tail factor is \(e^{u(p)}\), giving \(e^{1{,}645}=\) {{c2}} and \(e^{3{,}090}=\) {{c3}}.

Op risk has no balance-sheet exposure, so its regulatory proxy is {{c1}} — a {{c2}} (income), not a stock (assets) — sourced from {{c3}} reporting. By CRR Art. 4(1)(52) operational risk also explicitly includes {{c4}} (legal risk).
Derive the 5,0% Problemfall factor from the 15% Extremfall anchor under the ⅓-normal / ⅔-lognormal mixture (vertical VaR consistency, M4).

steps.prompt: Lognormal-two-thirds 95%/99,9% ratio, using e^1,645 and e^3,090 = ?
steps.explain: The lognormal stretches the tail (factor ~4,24 from 95% to 99,9% vs ~1,88 for normal), so its ratio is tiny.
Even though the lognormal carries the larger weight, its 0,236 ratio drags the blend down to ≈⅓.
Same M4 engine as CVA, but applied to a non-normal mixture, so the scalar is 0,333 not a single normal ratio.

cards.front: Claim: 'Both the 15% Extremfall factor and the 5,0% Problemfall factor for op risk are CRR-mandated regulatory values.' Classify the spine of each number and produce the tradeoff that distinguishes them.
rubric: Splits the claim: the 15% Extremfall factor is REGULATORY (the fixed CRR Basisindikatoransatz α on 3-yr average gross income, Art. 315–316; TSA betas 12–18% average ~15%).
The 5,0% Problemfall factor is an ÖRS CHOICE: a rescaling under the self-chosen ⅓-normal/⅔-lognormal mixture, not a CRR coefficient.

Names the tradeoff: CRR fixes the 99,9% anchor (comparability/Basel calibration), but the RTFA needs a 95% number, so the ÖRS supplies a proportionality model — adequacy justified by the RBG's low-beta retail/commercial business mix.
Rejects calling 5% 'regulatory' (it has no CRR coefficient) and rejects calling 15% an 'ÖRS invention' (it is the fixed Basel α).

cards.front: An analyst rescales the 15% op-risk charge to 95% using \(15\%\cdot\tfrac{1{,}645}{3{,}090}=8{,}0\%\), arguing 'the vertical VaR consistency from M4 gives a single quantile ratio.' Is 8,0% or 5,0% correct, and produce the tradeoff that decides it.
rubric: Verdict: 5,0% is correct; 8,0% is the wrong normal-only rescaling.
Identifies the error: 8,0% treats op-risk loss as purely normal (like CVA), but op risk has a fat right tail and is modelled ⅔ lognormal.

Produces the tradeoff: the lognormal 95%/99,9% ratio is only 0,236 vs 0,532 for the normal, so the blended ratio 0,333 (not 0,532) applies — the fat tail makes the 95% loss a much smaller share of the 99,9% loss.
Quantifies the consequence: on €20m, 8% gives €1,6m vs the correct €1,0m — an overstatement of ~60%.

cards.front: Board viva: 'Walk us through why the Problemfall operational-risk factor is 5,0% and not the ~8,0% a normal rescaling of 15% would give. How does this relate to the CVA factor 0,71 from M7?'

rubric.text: Names the engine: vertical VaR consistency (M4) — rescale by the 95%/99,9% quantile ratio.
States the op-risk distribution is a ⅓-normal / ⅔-lognormal mixture, with the lognormal capturing the fat right tail.
Gives the component ratios: normal 1,645/3,090=0,532, lognormal 5,180/21,982=0,236; blended 0,33·0,532+0,67·0,236=0,333.
Concludes 15%·0,333=5,0%; a normal-only ratio would wrongly give 15%·0,532=8,0%.
Contrasts with CVA: same M4 engine, but CVA is a pure normal VaR so its scalar is a single ratio 1,645/2,326=0,71, whereas op risk needs a mixture scalar.

antiPoints: Claiming 8,0% is correct / that op risk is rescaled as a pure normal VaR.
Attributing the difference to a holding-period change (250 days) or a different confidence level (99% vs 95%).
Saying the lognormal weight raises the factor — it lowers it, because its 95%/99,9% ratio is small.
cards.modelAnswer: Op risk uses the same M4 vertical VaR consistency as CVA — rescale the 99,9% charge by the 95%/99,9% quantile ratio — but op-risk loss is not normal: the Leitfaden models it as ⅓ normal plus ⅔ lognormal to respect the fat right tail of rare large losses. The normal third has ratio 1,645/3,090=0,532, but the lognormal two-thirds has ratio only 5,180/21,982=0,236, so the probability-weighted blend is 0,33·0,532+0,67·0,236=0,333, giving 15%·0,333=5,0%. A normal-only rescaling would wrongly yield 15%·0,532=8,0%, overstating the charge because the fat tail makes the 95% loss a far smaller share of the 99,9% loss. CVA differs only in distribution: it is treated as a pure normal VaR, so its scalar is the single ratio 1,645/2,326=0,71 — same engine, different tail.

cards.front: Board viva: 'Is the Leitfaden's 15%/5% (BIA-style) op-risk approach still current? What does CRR III change, and why does that matter?'

rubric.text: States the 15%/5% BIA-style approach post-dates and is superseded: CRR III (EU application from 1 Jan 2025) replaces BIA, TSA and AMA with a single Standardised Measurement Approach (SMA).
Gives SMA = BIC (Business Indicator Component) × ILM (Internal Loss Multiplier).
Explains the key economic change: the ILM adds loss-history sensitivity (10-year average losses) — a clean record can give ILM<1, a loss-heavy bank ILM>1 — which the flat 15% BIA lacks.
Flags this as a post-source item to verify against current CRR III / EBA, not a settled Leitfaden value.

antiPoints: Claiming CRR III leaves BIA/TSA unchanged or keeps the flat 15% factor.
Saying the SMA is loss-insensitive / identical to the BIA.
Confusing the BIC (a refined income/Business Indicator measure) with the old gross-income α only.
cards.modelAnswer: No — the Leitfaden's flat 15%/5% factor is BIA-style and post-dates the regime change, so it is superseded. Under CRR III (EU application from 1 January 2025) the Basisindikatoransatz, Standardansatz and Advanced Measurement Approach are all replaced by a single Standardised Measurement Approach: op-risk capital = BIC × ILM, where the Business Indicator Component is a marginal-coefficient function of a refined Business Indicator (interest, services and financial components) and the Internal Loss Multiplier scales it by the bank's own 10-year loss history. The economic upgrade is loss-history sensitivity — a bank with a clean record can earn ILM<1 while a loss-heavy one gets ILM>1 — which the flat 15% BIA cannot capture. This should be flagged as a post-source item and verified against current CRR III / EBA texts.
cards.sourceNote: Module §5.6 uses the BIA-style 15%/5% factor; CRR III (EU 2024/1623) op-risk SMA = BIC×ILM supersedes BIA/TSA/AMA from 2025. Card encodes the supersession as flagged in the module's CRR III box.

cards.front: An RTFA draft lists 'AML risk' and 'IT/IKT risk' as separate aggregated risk types alongside operational risk, and sizes op risk off total assets. Identify what is wrong and produce the structural tradeoff.
rubric: Both Geldwäsche/Terrorismusfinanzierung (AML/CFT) and IKT/ICT risk are COMPONENTS of operational risk, not standalone RTFA lines — op risk by CRR Art. 4(1)(52) also includes Rechtsrisiko.
Listing them separately double-counts and breaks the §5.6 structure; their losses (fines, remediation, legal, outages) fall under the same 15%/5% op-risk factor.
The indicator is wrong too: op-risk exposure scales with Betriebserträge (a flow / income), not with assets or RWA (a stock) — a bank can shrink assets yet keep the same op-risk surface.
Produces the tradeoff: the regulatory definition (CRR) fixes the perimeter (legal+IKT+AML inside op risk) and the income indicator, so deviating either double-counts capital or mis-sizes the charge.
